title: Computer Architecture & Operating Systems
blurb: How a computer actually runs your code -- CPU, memory, and the OS underneath everything.

lessons.title: The CPU & the instruction cycle
objectives: Explain the fetch-decode-execute cycle
Explain how fetch-decode-execute changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fetch-decode-execute with program counter and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A CPU repeatedly runs one cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory (using the program counter to know where), decode what it means, and execute it -- then repeat. Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations directly on the CPU, used to hold values mid-computation since accessing RAM is far slower than accessing a register.
examples:
# simplified instruction cycle, conceptually:
while True:
    instruction = fetch(program_counter)
    program_counter += 1
    operation, operands = decode(instruction)
    execute(operation, operands)  # e.g. add two register values
commonMistakes: Thinking of 'the CPU' as running your whole program in one step -- it's genuinely one tiny instruction at a time, repeated billions of times per second.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the foundational mental model every other computer engineering topic builds on -- interviewers expect you to know what's actually happening underneath a running program.

lessons.title: Memory hierarchy & cache
objectives: Explain why memory is organized in a hierarchy of speed vs size vs cost
Explain how memory hierarchy changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect memory hierarchy with cache and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Memory exists in a hierarchy: registers (fastest, tiniest), then cache (L1/L2/L3, small and fast), then RAM (larger, slower), then disk (largest, slowest).
examples:
# why this matters practically:
# looping over an array in memory order -> mostly cache hits, fast
# jumping randomly around a huge array -> mostly cache misses, much slower
# even though both do the 'same amount of work' by instruction count
commonMistakes: Assuming all memory access is equally fast -- a cache miss can be 100x slower than a cache hit, which is why data layout and access patterns matter so much for real performance.
lessons.careerRelevance: Cache-awareness separates code that merely works from code that performs well at scale -- a common systems-interview topic.

lessons.title: Processes vs threads
objectives: Distinguish a process from a thread and explain why the distinction matters
Explain how process changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect process with thread and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A process is a running program with its OWN isolated memory space -- one process can't directly read another's memory.
examples:
# process: your web browser (one process) and your text editor (a separate process) --
# neither can accidentally read the other's memory
# thread: your browser might use one thread for rendering the page and another
# for network requests -- both share the SAME browser process's memory
commonMistakes: Assuming threads are just 'lightweight processes' with no real difference -- the shared-memory aspect is exactly what causes race conditions, which isolated processes don't have to worry.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction underlies concurrency bugs, multiprocessing vs multithreading decisions, and is a near-universal systems interview question.

lessons.title: CPU scheduling algorithms
objectives: Compare FCFS and Round-Robin scheduling and their trade-offs
Explain how FCFS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect FCFS with Round-Robin and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: With one CPU and many processes wanting to run, the scheduler decides who runs when. First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) runs processes in arrival order to completion -- simple, but one long process can make everyone else wait a long time.
examples:
# FCFS: P1(10) then P2(5) then P3(8) -- P3 waits 15 time units before even starting
# Round-Robin (quantum=4): P1 runs 4, P2 runs 4, P3 runs 4, P1 runs its remaining 6, etc --
# every process gets SOME CPU time quickly, instead of waiting for the one ahead of it to fully finish
commonMistakes: Assuming a 'fair' scheduler means every process finishes at the same time -- fairness here means every process gets REGULAR turns, not equal total runtime.
lessons.careerRelevance: Scheduling trade-offs show up directly in real systems: thread pool design, task queues, and OS-level performance tuning.

lessons.title: Synchronization & deadlocks
objectives: Explain race conditions, locks, and the conditions that cause deadlock
Explain how race condition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect race condition with lock and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When multiple threads share memory, a race condition happens when the outcome depends on unpredictable timing of which thread runs first -- a lock (mutex) prevents this by letting only one thread access a shared resource at a time.
examples:
# classic deadlock: Thread A holds Lock 1, wants Lock 2.
# Thread B holds Lock 2, wants Lock 1.
# Neither can ever proceed -- this is deadlock.
# Fix: always acquire locks in the SAME consistent order across all threads.
commonMistakes: Adding locks to fix a race condition without considering lock ORDER across different threads -- inconsistent lock ordering is the most common real cause of deadlock.
lessons.careerRelevance: Race conditions and deadlocks are some of the hardest real bugs to find (see the Debugging course's coverage of flaky bugs) -- and a classic systems-interview topic.

lessons.title: Virtual memory & paging
objectives: Explain how virtual memory lets each process believe it has its own full address space
Explain how virtual memory changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect virtual memory with page and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Virtual memory gives each process its own private address space, translated by the OS and hardware into real physical memory addresses -- this is why one process can't accidentally read another's memory, and why a program can use addresses that don't correspond to where its data is actually, physically stored.
examples:
# virtual address -> split into a page number and an offset within that page
# page number looked up in the page table -> physical page location
# offset added -> the exact physical byte address
# e.g. virtual address 4500 with 4096-byte pages -> page 1, offset 404
commonMistakes: Confusing virtual memory with 'using disk space as extra RAM' entirely -- that's swap space specifically, one PART of what virtual memory enables, not the whole concept.
lessons.careerRelevance: Virtual memory is why process isolation and memory safety work the way they do -- a foundational concept for understanding both security and performance.

lessons.title: Address spaces, segmentation & memory protection
objectives: Explain virtual address spaces, segmentation concepts, and why process memory is isolated
Explain how address space changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect address space with segmentation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A process uses virtual addresses that the operating system and hardware translate to physical memory. Historically, segmentation divided memory into logical regions with base/limit rules; modern general-purpose systems rely heavily on paging, while the idea of distinct code, data, heap, and stack regions remains useful.
lessons.example: Reasoning exercise: two processes can both use the same virtual address value while the page tables map those addresses to different physical frames. That is why equal virtual addresses do not imply shared memory.
commonMistakes: Treating segmentation and paging as identical.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

lessons.title: File systems, system calls & I/O
objectives: Trace how an application file operation crosses into the OS and reaches persistent storage
Explain how system call changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect system call with file descriptor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Applications request privileged operating-system work through system calls. Opening a file returns a handle/file descriptor; reads and writes move data through kernel-managed buffers and the file-system layer.
lessons.example: Conceptual flow: Python open() -> OS open system call -> file descriptor -> read/write calls -> page cache -> file-system/storage layer. Closing releases the descriptor; explicit durability may require a flush/fsync depending on guarantees needed.
commonMistakes: Assuming write() or closing a high-level file object always means the bytes are physically durable on disk at that exact moment.

description: How a computer actually runs your code -- CPU, memory, and the OS underneath everything.

quiz.q: What does the CPU do during the 'fetch' stage?
options: Retrieves the next instruction from memory

quiz.q: What is a register?
options: Extremely fast storage located directly on the CPU

quiz.q: Why is accessing a register faster than accessing RAM?
options: Registers use a different programming language
Registers are physically on the CPU, RAM is farther away and slower to reach

quiz.q: What is a cache hit?
options: The needed data was found in the faster cache instead of slower RAM

quiz.q: Why does cache hit rate matter so much for real-world performance?
options: A cache miss can be far slower than a hit, so access patterns heavily affect real speed
Cache hit rate only affects battery life

quiz.q: What best describes locality of reference?
options: Storing data physically near the user
Programs tend to access nearby memory locations close together in time
A type of virtual memory error

quiz.q: What distinguishes a process from a thread?
options: A process has its own isolated memory; threads within a process share that process's memory
Threads are always faster than processes

quiz.q: Why are threads considered 'lighter-weight' than processes?
options: Creating a thread doesn't require setting up a whole new isolated memory space
Threads run on a different CPU

quiz.q: What is a key risk introduced by threads sharing memory?
options: Race conditions from unpredictable timing between threads

quiz.q: What does First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling do?
options: Runs processes in arrival order, each to completion

quiz.q: What is a key downside of FCFS scheduling?
options: One long process can make everyone behind it wait a long time
It can never be used for real systems

quiz.q: What is a 'quantum' in Round-Robin scheduling?
options: A physics concept unrelated to computing
The fixed time slice each process gets before switching to the next

quiz.q: Why is Round-Robin often preferred for interactive systems over FCFS?
options: Every process gets regular turns quickly, instead of waiting for the process ahead to fully finish

quiz.q: What is a race condition?
options: An outcome that depends on unpredictable timing between threads accessing shared memory

quiz.q: What does a lock (mutex) do?
options: Ensures only one thread can access a shared resource at a time
Deletes race conditions permanently with no other planning needed

quiz.q: What is deadlock?
options: A program running out of memory
Two or more threads each holding a resource the other needs, so neither can proceed

quiz.q: What is the most common real-world cause of deadlock?
options: Inconsistent lock ordering across different threads

quiz.q: What does virtual memory give each process?
options: Its own private address space, translated to real physical memory by the OS/hardware
Direct access to every other process's memory

quiz.q: What is a page table used for?
options: Mapping virtual pages to their physical memory locations

quiz.q: What is a page fault?
options: When a needed page isn't currently in RAM and must be loaded, often from disk

quiz.q: Why is a page fault typically much slower than a normal memory access?
options: Loading from disk is far slower than accessing RAM directly
Page faults use more CPU registers
Page faults always crash the program

exercises.title: Trace an FCFS schedule
exercises.prompt: Given processes P1(6), P2(3), P3(9) arriving in that order under FCFS, what time does each process complete?
exercises.hint: P1 completes at 6, P2 at 9, P3 at 18 -- each starts right after the previous finishes

exercises.title: Trace a Round-Robin schedule
exercises.prompt: Given P1(5), P2(3) with quantum=2, write out the execution order (which process runs, start time, end time) until both finish.

exercises.title: Identify the deadlock condition
exercises.prompt: Thread A holds Lock X and wants Lock Y. Thread B holds Lock Y and wants Lock X. Explain why this deadlocks and how consistent lock ordering would prevent it.
exercises.hint: circular wait -- neither can proceed; if both always acquired X before Y, one would simply wait for the other to finish with X, no cycle

exercises.title: Translate a virtual address
exercises.prompt: Given a page size of 4096 bytes and virtual address 9000, compute the page number and offset.
exercises.hint: page_number = address // page_size, offset = address % page_size

exercises.title: Diagnose a cache-unfriendly access pattern
exercises.prompt: Two functions process the same 2D array: one iterates row-by-row (matching memory layout), the other column-by-column (jumping around memory). The second is much slower despite doing the same number of operations. Why?
exercises.hint: row-by-row access matches how the array is actually laid out in memory, so it mostly hits cache; column-by-column jumps around memory, causing many more cache misses

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through what happens, at a high level, when a CPU executes one instruction.
interviewPreparation.a: The CPU fetches the instruction from memory at the address the program counter points to, decodes what operation it represents, executes it (e.g. an arithmetic operation or a memory access), and advances the program counter -- then repeats, billions of times per second.

interviewPreparation.q: Why can a program with the same number of operations run much faster or slower depending on how it accesses memory?
interviewPreparation.a: Cache hit rate matters enormously -- accessing memory in a pattern that matches how it's laid out (sequential access) tends to hit the fast cache repeatedly, while jumping around unpredictably causes many slow cache misses that have to reach all the way to RAM.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between using multiple processes versus multiple threads for a concurrent task?
interviewPreparation.a: Processes are isolated -- safer from shared-state bugs, but heavier to create and communicate between. Threads share memory within a process -- lighter-weight and can share data directly, but introduce race-condition risk that requires careful synchronization (locks) to manage.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you explain deadlock to someone who's never heard the term, using a concrete example?
interviewPreparation.a: Two threads each hold something the other needs and won't give up -- like two people each holding one of two keys the other needs, standing still waiting for the other to hand theirs over first. Neither will move, so nothing happens. The fix is agreeing on a consistent order everyone acquires resources in, so this circular standoff can't occur.

interviewPreparation.q: Why does virtual memory exist, and what real problem does it solve?
interviewPreparation.a: It gives each process its own private, isolated address space translated to real physical memory by the OS and hardware -- this is what prevents one process from accidentally (or maliciously) reading or corrupting another process's memory, and lets each program behave as if it has a large, contiguous address space regardless of how physical memory is actually fragmented.

capstone.title: Build and benchmark a CPU scheduler against realistic workloads
capstone.description: Implement both FCFS and Round-Robin scheduling for a set of processes with varying burst times, then compare their average waiting time and turnaround time across several different workload shapes (some with many short processes, some with a few long ones) -- and write up which scheduler wins for which shape, and why.
deliverables: A working simulator implementing both FCFS and Round-Robin scheduling given arbitrary process lists
Computed average waiting time and turnaround time for each algorithm, across at least 3 different workload shapes
A short written comparison explaining which algorithm performed better for which workload shape, and why -- tied to the actual mechanics of each algorithm, not just the numbers
capstone.portfolioTips: Comparing scheduling algorithms across DIFFERENT workload shapes (not just one example) is what shows real understanding of the trade-offs, rather than having memorized that 'Round-Robin is fairer.'

industryUsage.usage: The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) is a real, production CPU scheduler balancing fairness and responsiveness across every process on a Linux machine, including the servers most backend services run on.
CPU cache hierarchy design (L1/L2/L3) is one of the most heavily engineered aspects of modern processors, directly because cache hit rate dominates real-world performance more than raw clock speed.
Database systems implement their own lock managers and deadlock detection internally, since concurrent transactions on shared data hit exactly the synchronization problems covered in this course.

careerApplications: Used by systems, backend, performance, and infrastructure engineers to reason about processes, memory, scheduling, files, concurrency, and how software interacts with the operating system.
